I’ve farmed these same plots in Quzhou for 50 years, so I know what works and what doesn’t. My wife and I are both getting on in years — just the two of us in the house now — so I can’t take big risks or wear myself out with heavy labor. I’ll plant all 10.1 mu to winter wheat in October, like I always do. I buy improved wheat seed from the shop in town because that’s what my neighbors grow and it’s reliable. For fertilizer, I put down about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu — I’ve learned that if I cut back too much the yield drops badly, but we also can’t afford to throw money away. I’ll irrigate three times: once before winter to help it settle, once at jointing when the wheat starts shooting up, and once at grain filling. The well water costs electricity, but without those irrigations the spring drought would ruin us. 

Come June, right after I harvest the wheat, the window to plant summer maize is only about a week, so I do no-tillage planting like everyone else in the village — there’s no time to plough. I always buy hybrid maize seed; the yield is so much better than saving your own. Maize needs a bit less fertilizer than wheat, maybe 14 kg nitrogen per mu, and I irrigate twice if the rains don’t come. I spray pesticide twice for each crop — herbicide once and insecticide once — that’s usually enough to keep the weeds and bugs under control. If the weather is normal, I expect about 430 kg per mu from the wheat and 510 kg per mu from the maize.
